Load the libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
options(scipen = 999)

Data

For this homework, we are going to use the Gapminder data on population (pop), GDP per capita (gdp), and life expectancy (lex). These data were downloaded and compiled using the gapminder_compile.Rmd script in the data folder.

Let’s focus our attention on data from the past 100 years, between 1925 and 2025.

gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder.csv") %>% 
  clean_names() %>% 
  filter(between(year, 1925, 2025))
  1. Use the function(s) of your choice to get an idea of the overall structure of the data, including its dimensions, column names, classes, etc.
summary(gapminder)
##    country               year           pop                  gdp

##  Class :character   1st Qu.:1950   1st Qu.:    741871   1st Qu.:  2124

names(gapminder)
## [1] "country" "year"    "pop"     "gdp"     "lex"
  1. How many countries are represented in this dataset?
gapminder %>% 
  distinct(country) %>% 
  count()
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##       n
##   <int>
## 1   195
  1. Which five countries have had the largest absolute population growth between 1925-2025? Show this as a table.
cent_pop_growth <- gapminder %>% 
  select(country, pop, year) %>% 
  filter(year %in% c(1925, 2025)) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = year,
              values_from = pop,
              names_prefix = "year_")%>% 
  mutate(pop_growth=year_2025-year_1925)

cent_pop_growth %>% 
  arrange(desc(pop_growth)) %>% 
  slice_head(n=5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 4
##   country   year_1925  year_2025 pop_growth
##   <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 India     304406019 1463865525 1159459506
## 2 China     473741473 1416096094  942354621
## 3 Indonesia  49685263  285721236  236035973
## 4 Pakistan   22624808  255219554  232594746
## 5 USA       116193761  347275807  231082046
  1. Make a plot that shows population growth over time for the top country you found in question #3.
gapminder %>% 
  filter(country=="India") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=pop)) +
  geom_line(color="tomato3")+
  geom_point(shape=5)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1925, 2025, by=5), minor_breaks = NULL)+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust=1))+
   labs(title = "Population Growth of India 1925-2025",
       x="Year",
       y="Population")

  1. Has global life expectancy changed between 1925 and 2025? Show the min, median, mean, and max for all countries (combined) in the dataset.
gapminder %>% 
  select(country, lex, year) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1925, 2025)) %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  summarise(min_lex=min(lex, na.rm=T),
            median_lex=median(lex, na.rm=T),
            mean_lex=mean(lex, na.rm=T),
            max_lex=max(lex, na.rm=T))
## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##    year min_lex median_lex mean_lex max_lex
##   <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1  1925    21.0       35.9     38.1    63.5
## 2  2025    52.8       74.8     73.9    85.6

Yes, global life expectancy has increased significantly in the last 100 years.

  1. Make a plot that shows the distribution of life expectancy for all countries in 1925 and 2025 (try using geom_density). What do you notice about the shift in life expectancy over time?
gapminder %>% 
  select(country, lex, year) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1925, 2025)) %>% 
  mutate(year=factor(year)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=lex, color=year, fill=year))+
  geom_density(alpha=0.4)+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")
## Warning: Removed 13 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_density()`).

Life expectancy has shifted to be significantly higher in 2025 than it was in 1925

  1. We are interested in the relationship between per capita GDP and life expectancy; i.e. does having more money help you live longer in 2025? Show this as a plot. (Suggestion! Remove Monaco as an extreme outlier.)
gapminder %>% 
  filter(year=="2025" & country!="Monaco") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=gdp, y=lex))+
  geom_point(shape=1)+
  geom_smooth(method=lm, se=F, color="tomato3")+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust=1))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 140000 , by=10000), minor_breaks = NULL)+
  labs(title = "Life Expectancy vs. GDP per Capita",
       x="GDP per Capita",
       y="Life Expectancy (years)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

This graph indicates a positive relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy, so yes having more money appears to lead to longer life.

  1. Which five countries have had the highest absolute GDP per capita growth over the past 50 years? Show this as a table. (Suggestion! Remove Monaco as an extreme outlier.)
gapminder %>% 
  select(year, gdp, country) %>% 
  filter(year %in% c(1975, 2025) & country != "Monaco") %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = year,
              values_from = gdp,
              names_prefix = "year_") %>% 
  mutate(gdp_growth=year_2025-year_1975) %>% 
  arrange(desc(gdp_growth))%>% 
  slice_head(n=5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 4
##   country    year_1975 year_2025 gdp_growth
##   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 Singapore     12896.   137906.    125010.
## 2 Ireland       14336.   119406.    105071.
## 3 Luxembourg    30950.   131038.    100088.
## 4 Guyana         5071.    79371.     74300.
## 5 Norway        25513.    94896.     69382.
  1. How does per capita GDP growth compare between these same five countries over the past 50 years? Show this as a plot.
gapminder %>% 
  filter(country=="Singapore" |
        country=="Ireland" |
        country=="Luxembourg" |
        country=="Guyana" |
        country=="Norway",
        year>=1975) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=gdp, color=country))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(shape=1)+
  scale_colour_brewer(palette="Set2")+
  labs(title = "GDP per capita growth for top 5 countries 1975-2025",
       x="Year",
       y="GDP")

  1. Do one analysis of your choice that includes a table and plot as outputs.

Change in life expectancy in the past 25 years of the countries with the largest populations in 2025.

gapminder %>% 
  select(country, pop, year) %>% 
  filter(year=="2025") %>% 
  arrange(desc(pop)) %>% 
  slice_head(n=5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   country          pop  year
##   <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 India     1463865525  2025
## 2 China     1416096094  2025
## 3 USA        347275807  2025
## 4 Indonesia  285721236  2025
## 5 Pakistan   255219554  2025
gapminder %>% 
  filter(country=="India" |
         country=="China"|
         country=="USA"|
         country=="Indonesia"|
         country=="Pakistan",
         year>="2000") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=lex, color=country))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(shape=5)+
  scale_colour_brewer(palette="Set3")+
  labs(title = "25 year trends in life expectancy of countries with largest populations in 2025",
       x="Year",
       y="Life Expectancy (years")

There appears to be a dip in life expectancy around the Covid pandemic, pretty severe ones in the case of India and Indonesia. Indonesia and Pakistan also saw dips in life expectancy around 2004 and 2005 respectively.
